subject: Framework for simulation study to validate bayesian models

messages.author: 39971e2c19b8ec70
messages.subject: Framework for simulation study to validate bayesian models
parts:
Hi guys,

I am looking for a framework that would allow to take JAGS/bugs model
and on many sets of simulated data test if there is a bias (or not) in
the parameter estimates (the real parameters would be known because
the data are simulated). Is there any such framework? I've seen only
`run.jags.study()` in R package `runjags`, but this is focused on
crossvalidation. I need to check the bias in parameter estimates.

Or, can you remind me a chapter in one of Marc's book which focuses on
that? :-) I am especially interested how to evaluate the bias across
the generated data sets.

Thanks in advance!

Tomas

messages.author: d647e6438dc3aad6
messages.subject: Re: Framework for simulation study to validate bayesian models
parts:
Hi Tomas,

It sounds like you want to run a standard model-validation exercise. The process is similar regardless of the type of model you want to fit, and I'm sure there are R packages available to help with this, although I haven't used any. I would perform the following steps:

1. Simulate the data (1000 times or so, or probably a minimum of 100 if your model takes very long to run). You can simulate the data in base R or your package/program of choice - no need to simulate in a BUGS framework. Chapter 4 of Kery & Royle (vol 1) could help with this.

2. To each simulated dataset, fit your BUGS model, making sure to output the estimates of the parameters that you want to validate.

3. Across all the simulated datasets, check how many times the 95% BCI of each estimate contains your true value. If the 95% BCI excludes the true value >5% of the time, you have a bias (probably a big one if your 95% BCI is fairly wide). You can check whether the true value is above or below each BCI to evaluate the direction of the bias. 

4. As an additional way to evaluate the estimates, across all the simulated datasets, take the mean of the parameter estimate and calculate a 95% CI based on the SD across datasets. If the 95% CI excludes your true value, you have a bias. (This is mixing Bayesian and frequentist paradigms, which is not ideal, and I hope someone will correct me if this comparison will be fundamentally flawed - I've only implemented it in a purely frequentist framework. My thought is that it might detect smaller biases than could be detected from the 95% BCI, if there is high uncertainty in the model, as is common in a Bayesian framework. But perhaps precision around the mean could be overestimated with this method, especially with many replicates, so it would be worth considering the biological significance of any bias.)

I would personally run step 2 in JAGS with runjags as usual for any model/dataset, and use base R for the other steps. I'll look forward to hearing suggestions from anyone who knows an efficient R package or has any BUGS-specific advice.

Cheers,

Emily
